text: Privacy by Design isn't a law — it's a design philosophy. Seven principles, developed by Ann Cavoukian, for building privacy into a system's architecture from day one, instead of bolting it on after the fact.

Principle one: proactive, not reactive — prevent privacy problems before they happen. Principle two: privacy as the default setting — protection without the user having to ask for it. Principle three: privacy embedded into design — a core part of the architecture, not an add-on feature.

Principle four: full functionality — positive-sum, not zero-sum. You shouldn't have to trade away features or security to get privacy. Principle five: end-to-end security, across the entire data lifecycle. Principle six: visibility and transparency — practices that are verifiable, not hidden in fine print.

Principle seven: respect for user privacy — stay user-centric. And here's where this becomes law: GDPR Article 25 requires "data protection by design and by default" — this exact philosophy, written directly into binding EU regulation.

Retrofitting privacy into a system never built for it is expensive and incomplete. Building these seven principles in from day one makes privacy a property of the architecture itself. That closes out this chapter — Chapter 2 moves into how sensitive data actually gets classified.
